newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan stocks to seek clues to new coalition.
newsitem.headline: Japan stocks to seek clues to new coalition.

text.p: The Tokyo stock market is likely to want to see the shape of Japan's next coalition government before handing down final judgment on the results of Sunday's election, brokers and economists said on Sunday.

Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto looked set to head the next government, but said he needed coalition partners after his conservative Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) appeared likely to fall short of a clear majority.
Share prices rose last week after media polls said the LDP, the biggest party in the outgoing ruling bloc, had a good chance to win a simple majority in the powerful Lower House.
Some analysts said share prices might fall in disappointment at the LDP's failure to win a simple majority and due to concern over how long it might take the party to build a working coalition.
"It's not as expected, since the LDP has not obtained one-party rule, which was the hype in the stock market last week," said Jesper Koll, chief economist at JP Morgan in Tokyo.
"There is uncertainty, and uncertainty means sell."
Robert Feldman, chief economist at Salomon Brothers Asia, also said the stock market might be disappointed by the LDP's failure to gain a simple majority.
"They're going to have trouble putting together a coalition," Feldman said. "It's not clear to me where major economic policies are going."

Some said, however, that the market might take comfort from the fact that the LDP would be in the driver's seat in the next coalition government. "The market has already factored in an LDP victory and now the LDP is certain to take the lead in any coalition," said Masaaki Higashida, a strategist at Nomura Securities Co Ltd. "The results of the election are not likely to have a big impact on the market," he added, speaking before final results had been announced.

Analysts agreed that the market would want to see the exact shape of the next coalition, as well as what economic policies the next government would come up with and whether those policies would be implemented smoothly.

Among the looming problems to be dealt with are the budget for 1997/98, tax reform, deregulation, and the burden on public coffers of Japan's rapidly ageing population. "The question is -- with whom will the LDP link up," said Yasuo Ueki, a general manager at Nikko Securities Co Ltd.
"Share prices won't go up and they won't go down," Ueki said, also speaking ahead of final tallies.
Nomura's Higashida said the stock market might also be concerned by the record low turnout in Sunday's election.
"The low turnout is probably a reflection of the fact that the electorate has no expectations of any politicians, and that view may also exist in the market," he said.

Japan's government bond market was likely to be interested in whether the LDP fulfilled promises by some leaders of a five trillion yen supplementary budget for the fiscal year to March 31, 1997, analysts said. "The real question is whether there will be serious fiscal reform efforts, but that won't affect the market on a day-to-day basis," Feldman said.
